# Bacteria game

Rules for working on `libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game`, on top of the repo's
`CLAUDE.md`.

The engine (the match, its simulation, replays, levels, progress and the
English texts it renders itself) is the lib `feat-shared-bacteria-engine`
(`libs/features/bacteria-engine`, see its `CLAUDE.md`). Paths below that
start with `state/` are in that lib unless they name one of the five
Angular files that stay here (`game-state.service.ts`, `game.states.ts`,
`match-recorder.ts`, `player.service.ts`, `player.store.ts`) or `match-rules.ts`. The game imports the engine only
through `@wolsok/feat-shared-bacteria-engine` and its entries (`/cloud`, and
`/gpu` in specs and the bench).

The arena rendering and the GPU simulation (`gl/`, `arena/`, `player-color.ts`,
`reduced-motion.ts`, the GPU cross-check in `gpu-crosscheck/`) are the lib
`feat-bacteria-rendering` (`libs/features/bacteria-rendering`, #3102); paths
below starting with `gl/` or `arena/` are in its `src/lib/`. It imports
nothing of the game, and the game takes it only through
`@wolsok/feat-bacteria-rendering`. The services that tie the GPU choice to the
game's device storage and analytics, `GpuSelfTestService` and
`SimulationOverrideService`, stay here in `gpu-choice/`, with
`simulation-check.ts`, whose lines are the game's settings texts.

The sound (the Web Audio synth, the level and menu music, the step
scheduler) is the lib `feat-bacteria-sound` (`libs/features/bacteria-sound`,
#3102), taken through `@wolsok/feat-bacteria-sound`. It reads the sound
settings through its port `SoundSettings`; `sound/game-sound.service.ts`
here is the root `GameSoundService`, a `GameSound` over the device settings
(`soundSettingsOf`).

## Persistence: local storage or Firebase, behind ports

The game keeps the player's progress (medallions, campaign, XP, achievements,
totals) in its own Firebase project once one is configured, and in local
storage until then. Settings stay with the device either way.

- Everything the game stores goes through a port in `src/lib/storage/`.
  Nothing else touches `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB or Firebase
  directly.
  - `GameStorage` is the player's storage and follows their account:
    `FirestoreGameStorage` with a project, `LocalGameStorage` without.
  - `DeviceStorage` is this device's storage, always `LocalGameStorage`. The
    settings (`GameSettingsService`) live there, so sound, controls and
    graphics stay per device whoever signs in. Each device setting is one
    entry of `SETTINGS` (`settings/setting-table.ts`: default, `parse` of
    the stored value, `normalize`, `reported`), read and changed through
    `value(key)`, `set(key, v)` and `preview(key, v)`; `DeviceSettings`
    restores, keeps and stores all of them alike, `StoredMatchSetup` the
    match setup beside them. A new setting is a new entry (and a sample
    in `device-settings.spec.ts`), no new signal or setter.
  - `GameAccount` says who plays (`FirebaseGameAccount`, or `DeviceAccount`
    without a project) and signs in and out. Its `owner` (the admin claim,
    a verified email and a Google sign-in in the current token) only shows
    the main menu's way to `/admin` on the game's own site.
- The project is named with `provideGameCloud(environment.gameCloud)` in the
  providers of the remote's entry route, not in its app config: inside the
  shell only the entry routes are loaded. The game's services sit in the root
  injector and would not see a provider on that route, so `GameStorage` and
  `GameAccount` ask the root `GameCloud`, which the route's initializer sets
  before the game starts. `gameCloud: null` keeps everything local.
- Firebase comes through AngularFire (`@angular/fire`): `provideGameCloud`
  provides the game's own named app (`bacteria-wars`), Auth and Firestore on
  that route, where they stand in for the shell's, which belong to another
  project. The backends call the Firebase SDK itself on the injected
  instances, not AngularFire's wrapped functions: the app is zoneless, where
  the wrapping only adds pending tasks (a write held offline keeps the app
  from turning stable), and it wraps every function argument as a callback,
  which breaks the popup resolver class.
- Online matches meet through the `GameRooms` port (`storage/game-rooms.ts`,
  `FirestoreGameRooms`), asked of `GameCloud.rooms()` - null without a
  project. The match itself goes device to device (`net/`), never through
  Firestore. Once the link opened, the host swaps the room for its stub
  (`OpenRoom.take`, ADR 0011), which the functions bind an online replay's
  players to: without it every online upload is refused. Only a room
  nobody joined is deleted (`close`). `OnlineMatchService` reaches the
  other device through the `PeerTransport` port (`net/peer-transport.ts`,
  token `PEER_TRANSPORT`): `WebRtcTransport` (`net/peer-link.ts`) in the
  game, `pairedTransport()` with `FakeGameRooms` (`src/testing/`) in specs,
  where two real services play the protocol against each other. Specs of
  what uses the online match provide `FakeOnlineMatch` (`src/testing/`).
- Profiles, friends, challenges and the matchmaking queue go through the
  `GameSocial` port (`storage/game-social.ts`, `FirestoreGameSocial`), the
  online status through `GamePresence` (`RtdbGamePresence`, the Realtime
  Database) - `GameCloud.social()` and `.presence()`, null without a
  project or its database. `SocialService` is the one place the game reads
  them from; specs use `FakeGameSocial` and `FakeGamePresence`
  (`src/testing/`). It watches a friend's status only while the
  friendship is mutual: the status becomes readable by friends only (ADR
  0012, owner's decision of 2026-10-26), a refused read ends the Realtime
  Database listener, so `RtdbGamePresence.watch` listens again a few
  times (the functions write the reader mirror a few seconds late). A new
  status read follows the same rule.
- The leaderboards (ADR 0012) are read through the `GameBoards` port
  (`storage/game-boards.ts`, `FirestoreGameBoards`), asked of
  `GameCloud.boards()` - null without a project - and only by
  `BoardsService` (`boards/`). The functions write every board; the game
  only reads: the top document live, pages of `entries` (`status in`
  `VISIBLE_STATUSES`, ordered `sort` desc, `atHour` asc, the document id,
  as the one entries index and the rules want; a new query goes into
  `GAME_QUERIES` in `apps/bacteria-game-remote/src/firestore-indexes.spec.ts`),
  and the player's own row from `boardMembers/{uid}`: `boards` says which
  boards they are on (the entry ids exist for every kind at once), a
  refused `get` of their entry reads as hidden, a missing one (the rules
  let it through as not found) as no counted result yet, and a position
  below the top 50 is one `count()`. An own row
  the owner hides says it is hidden, never that it does not count (ADR
  0012, owner's decision of 2026-10-25). Specs use `FakeGameBoards` and
  its `topRowsOf` (`src/testing/`). The main menu shows the screen with the
  cloud while the `leaderboards` toggle is on.
- The match on the board is recorded by `MatchRecorder`
  (`state/match-recorder.ts`): `GameStateService` calls `begin` with the
  plan and how the match records as its colonies spawn, the engine samples
  through `sample`, and `finish` scores the replay, sets `lastRecording`
  (what the replay screens read) and submits it. It reads the engine only
  through the `MatchTape` port, which `PlayerService` fills, so its specs
  play a `MatchEngine` instead of the whole service. The settings hand it
  the replay preferences (`setPrefs`, from `syncReplayPrefs` only).
- Recorded matches (ADR 0011) go through the `GameReplays` port
  (`storage/game-replays.ts`), asked of `GameCloud.replays()`:
  `FirestoreGameReplays` once the project takes them
  (`GameCloudOptions.replays`, on in the remote's production and emulator
  environments), else `LocalGameReplays` on this device (the newest 20);
  `cloud` tells which. The client never writes `replays`: it writes
  `replaySubmissions` and `replayCommands`, which the functions carry out,
  and reads its own replays back (`listMine`, one query in `GAME_QUERIES`).
  `listingOf` reads the functions' fields of `replays/{id}` - the seat from
  `seats` (online, host 0), `rankedReason` (`ARRIVAL_REASONS`,
  `ONLINE_REASONS` in `state/replay/replay-reasons.ts`, exported by the engine,
  where the functions take their reason types from),
  `galleryOut`, `publicId` - and leaves out what it does not know. A new
  reason needs its text in the `replay.reasons` area (a `satisfies` there
  fails to compile without it). In the cloud
  `remove` ("Keep out of the gallery") keeps a match out of the gallery
  and deletes nothing; "Delete" sends `forget` (ADR 0012, owner's
  decision of 2026-10-26): the functions take the player out of the
  replay (`players`, seats) and its public copies, so it leaves
  `listMine`, while the replay stays anonymised for the statistics.
  `FirestoreGameReplays` sends it while a ban holds, as the rules allow;
  it answers `ranking` while the boards may still rank the match (the
  screen says it can be deleted later) and `not-found` for one that no
  longer names the player (read as deleted). On this device both delete
  for real. "Delete" takes two taps, like the HUD's "Give up", both
  through `armedTap` (`armed-tap.ts`): the first arms that match's button
  for `ARMED_MS` (3 s), the second deletes; the button stays the same
  element, so keyboard focus stays on it. The privacy page (`apps/bacteria-game-remote/src/app/privacy`)
  says what each does: keep it in step. "My matches" (`replays/my-matches.component.ts`)
  and the match just played (`replay-screen.component.ts`) are stage
  screens; specs use `FakeGameReplays` (`cloud`, `change` and
  `forgetAnswer`).
- The result screen's replay note (`replays/replay-note.component.ts`)
  says once per device, after the first match against the computer the
  cloud saved (not online, not ranked), that such matches are saved and
  that Settings -> Matches turns it off (owner's decision of 2026-10-26:
  recording stays on by default). The device setting
  `recordingHintShown` keeps it shown; the note decides only once
  `GameSettingsService.loaded` says the stored settings are read.
- A local match against the computer is recorded on every simulation
  resolution (owner's decision of 2026-10-26) and goes to `GameReplays` on
  every one of them too (owner's decision of 2026-10-31): the stored parse
  takes any grid of the level (`simGridOf`, `state/replay/replay.ts`), an online
  or ranked match only the online grid. On the online grid a recorded
  match plays a ruleset (`recordedSeats` in `PlayerService.init`: `cpu`
  where the device would pick the float GPU); on another grid it plays
  what the device picks unrecorded, and a float GPU match leaves no
  recording - recording never moves a match off the GPU there. The viewer
  lays a replay out on its own grid (`simResolutionOf`,
  the engine's `state/simulation/arena-size.ts`); the functions scale a re-run's expected cost by
  the arena's cells (`expectedRerunMs`) and count the level statistics
  per grid (`levelStatsKey`, `simGridOf` from the engine lib).
- Ranked daily attempts and endless runs (ADR 0012) are declared through
  the `GameRanked` port (`storage/game-ranked.ts`, `FirestoreGameRanked`),
  asked of `GameCloud.ranked()` - null without a project - and only by
  `RankedService` (`ranked/`). A declaration is a transaction (it fails
  offline instead of waiting in the cache) that writes
  `{ at: serverTimestamp(), expireAt }` and nothing else - what the rules'
  `isDeclaration` wants - then reads `at` back with `getDocFromServer`,
  3 s in all (`DECLARE_TIMEOUT_MS`; past it one more read from the server
  takes a declaration that committed late), `at` floored to whole ms
  (`millisOf`, `storage/firestore-values.ts`) as the server reads it; the
  seed is `attemptSeed(uid, id, at)`, the match `rankedPlan` on the online
  grid, on the level of the attempt's own day, `gpu-int`, no restart and
  no pause (the deadline runs from the declaration; the HUD's "Give up",
  two taps, is its way out), uploaded whatever the
  recording settings say, with the attempt in the header and the
  submission. Ranked play is offered by
  the owner's toggles (`rankedDaily`, `rankedEndless`: off hides the
  switch) on a device whose GPU passed the self-test and has the integer
  passes (`deviceReady`), to a signed-in player no ban holds; the
  player's choice is the device setting `ranked`. The store's `next`
  holds the start's outcome in its `daily` and `endless` variants
  (`ranked`, read as `matchRules().ranked`): the declared match
  (`matchRules().rankedMatch`) and what the result screen says of it
  (`note`, ids, texts in `boards.ranked`).
  Specs use `FakeGameRanked`.
- The owner's moderation reaches the player through the `GameModeration`
  port (`storage/game-moderation.ts`, `FirestoreGameModeration`), asked
  of `GameCloud.moderation()` and read by `ModerationService`
  (`moderation/`): `bans/{uid}` live with its Realtime Database mirror
  (either holding is a ban, ended by itself at `until`) and
  `players/{uid}/notices`, deleted when dismissed. A ban takes away what
  the rules' `notBanned()` refuses: `FirestoreGameStorage` holds the
  player's writes until it ends (as offline), `FirestoreGameReplays`
  sends nothing, `SocialService` writes nothing and takes the status
  back, matchmaking stops, the lobby, profile editor and friends shut,
  ranked play is refused. A new client write path follows the ban too.
  Specs use `FakeGameModeration`.
- Specs provide the game cloud with `provideFakeGameCloud({ … })`
  (`src/testing/fake-game-cloud.ts`): a `GameCloud` without a project,
  every backend left out null (or on this device), never a hand-built
  object.
- The replay viewer (`replays/replay-viewer.component.ts`) plays a
  `ReplayScene` (`replay-scene.ts`) on an `ArenaViewComponent` by itself
  (its frames drawn by `arenaContent`, `arena/arena-content.ts`, like the
  game's):
  its own `MatchEngine` from `replayEngine` (`state/replay/replay.ts`, beside
  `canPlayBack` and `playReplay`, which the engine's `replayVerdict`,
  the functions' verification, builds on: keep their signatures; which
  parsed replays play back, and why not, is `playbackRefusal` alone, which
  `canPlayBack` and `replayVerdict` ask), nothing of the game's state. A
  `gpu-int` replay plays on the viewer's own GL painter (the third
  argument of `replayEngine`) where its renderer is the host's `gpu`
  (`GpuSelfTestService.trustedRenderer`: "My matches" and the match just
  played; `/watch` takes it from `WatchGpu` (`replays/watch-gpu.ts`,
  #3059): the game's stored verdict, read from local storage through
  `@wolsok/utils-browser-storage`, or the self-test run there on idle and
  stored the same way; the record's shape and rules are
  `gl/stored-self-test.ts`, shared with `GpuSelfTestService`). The viewer
  shows whether the war runs on the GPU or the CPU (`data-testid="engine"`).
  `ReplayScene.useGpu` moves the war between the GPU and the CPU where it
  was: onto the painter once it is there, off it before its context goes;
  a GPU that fails to set up falls back to `intSimulation` and is not
  asked again.
  The timeline and the 10 s buttons seek (`ReplayScene.seek`): the war only
  plays forwards, so back restarts it, and the frames after a seek play on
  to its tick within `SEEK_FRAME_MS` each, the view running while paused.
  The viewer is a video player: it fills the box it is given (the stage's
  screen, the `/watch` page), fits the arena into it by width and height,
  and lays its controls over the arena, which hide a few seconds into
  playback (`CHROME_HIDE_MS`); the controls, the keys and the fullscreen
  (on its own element) are listed in the component's JSDoc. The match just
  played and "My matches" show it alone on the screen (`:host.playing`,
  `screen.player`), the list or the header only while nothing plays.
  Specs draw with `recordingPainters` and play `recordedReplay` (`src/testing/`).
- `/watch/{publicId}` (the remote's `app.routes.ts`, outside the entry
  route with the cloud) loads `WatchPageComponent` from the narrow entry
  `@wolsok/feat-lazy-bac-game/watch` (`src/watch.ts`), skipped by
  federation like `admin-kit`. Keep that entry free of the stage, the
  storage backends and Firebase: it reaches the public replay through
  `loadPublicReplay` (`storage/public-replays.ts`, plain `fetch` of
  `/replays/{id}/replay.json`, base64 `bytes`), nothing else. An oxlint
  override in `.oxlintrc.json` guards the imports of the files it pulls
  in; a new one goes into its `files`.
- The profile's `publicName`, `boardOptOut` and `galleryOptOut` (all off
  by default) are saved by `FirestoreGameSocial.saveProfile` with
  `mergeFields`: only the fields the player changed (a first profile
  whole), each whole (an avatar must not merge into the last one), and
  nothing else touched. The editor's switches and save wait for
  `SocialService.profileLoaded`: the stored profile read, or the server's
  word that there is none (`watchProfile` holds back a miss only the cache
  tells), so the defaults shown meanwhile never overwrite stored flags.
- The owner's feature toggles (ADR 0012) come through the `GameToggles`
  port (`storage/game-toggles.ts`): `RemoteConfigGameToggles` with a

    medallion is kept, never a worse one, and an achievement keeps its
    earliest day. Such a change comes to the same however late or often a
    backend applies it.
  - Counts (the lifetime totals) are added to the stored value, never taken
    from memory, which misses what the storage has not told yet. An adding
    change must land exactly once, so `FirestoreGameStorage` runs `update` as
    a transaction, queued per key. Offline, the change waits to be online and
    runs then. The queue lives in memory, and a transaction never reaches
    Firestore's persistent cache: a change not committed when the page
    closes is lost there, online too. So `playerDocument` keeps what the
    page held after each change in `DeviceStorage` under `<key>.unsaved`

    only gain; a document whose changes cannot be merged that way must not
    go through `playerDocument`.

    cannot be merged so: `playerDocument` keeps it under `<key>.adoptions`

    the account's next start on the device lands what is left with
    `update(..., { once: id })`, which Firestore skips for an id it listed
    in `applied` (#3036).

- `playerIds` follows `players` from the same replaying subject, which keeps

  that guest.
- The first cloud player adopts what this device kept in local storage

## Online matches: keep the engine deterministic

`OnlineSeatSync` (`net/online-seat-sync.ts`) keeps this device's seat in
step with the other one: it follows `OnlineMatchService.events$`, owns the
colour handshake (the guest offers its pick, the host makes the pair and
shares the setup), starts the match (`matchStart`) and hands its changes
to `GameStateService` as patches (`changes$`), which applies them and
ends the match when the connection goes.

Online matches run in lockstep (`net/lockstep.ts`, ADR 0009): both devices
play the same `MatchEngine` from the same seed and the same inputs. Anything
that changes what a tick does from those - a `Math.random`, the wall clock,
a frame delta, a value only one device has - desyncs every online match, as
it breaks replays. Inputs reach the engine only on the input grid
(`onGrid`, `STEER_STEPS`, `DRAG_STEPS`), and `NET_VERSION` follows
`BALANCE_VERSION`, so two devices with different balance tables refuse to
play each other.

## Balance: the lab and the ladder's computer (ADR 0016)

- Against the computer on the ladder and on generated levels the menus
  pass loadouts and `ladder: LADDER_VERSION` in the plan: the computer then
  plays its place on the difficulty curve (`state/match/difficulty-curve.ts`) and
  carries `computerLoadout` (`state/match/computer-opponent.ts`). Such a replay
  is version 4. A change to `SKILL`, `STRENGTH`, the bands or a rule only the ladder's
  profiles switch on (`attacksAtCap`, `pushesAfterCryo`) changes those matches,
  as does one to what the computer buys (its budget, a character, the gene
  or weapon costs it spends along): raise `LADDER_VERSION` and take the new
  fingerprints in `golden-match.spec.ts`. A plain match must not move (`BALANCE_VERSION`).
- The balance lab (`state/balance/`, runner `tools/bacteria-game/balance/`)
  plays the stand-in (`REFERENCE_PROFILE`) against that computer. A change
  to the balance, the levels, the bots or the curve re-checks it:
  `nx run feat-shared-bacteria-engine:balance-check` (short, against the
  committed `state/balance/balance-report.json`); a new baseline with
  `tsx --tsconfig tools/tsconfig.tools.json tools/bacteria-game/balance/run.ts full --update` (hours; nightly on
  GitHub, `.github/workflows/bacteria-balance.yml`).

## The deterministic simulation (ADR 0015)

- `GridWar` (`state/simulation/grid/grid-war.ts`) is the grid war's bookkeeping,
  alike on every processor: walls, zones, pellets, effects, the frame's
  uniforms and what a report means. Change it there, once. It runs over the
  `CellPasses` port (`state/simulation/grid/cell-passes.ts`), whose adapters only run
  the cell passes and render the report: `IntReferencePasses` (the
  TypeScript reference, `intReferenceTick` and `intReport`; built by the
  engine's `intSimulation`) and the game's `GpuCellPasses`
  (`gl/gpu-cell-passes.ts`) with `GpuIntRules` or `GpuFloatRules`
  (`gl/gpu-rules.ts`; built by `gpuSimulation`, `gl/gpu-simulation.ts`).
  What tells the integer GPU passes from the float ones lives in the rules
  only. Adapters read nothing of the war but what the calls hand them, and
  hand their reports back through the `ReportSink`; `grid-war.spec.ts`
  checks the bookkeeping on a stub port. The map, pellets, effects, moving
  walls and the tick's events are `ArenaFixtures`
  (`state/simulation/arena-fixtures.ts`), shared with `BacteriaSimulation`.
- A change to the integer passes, the report or the uniforms has to land in
  the shaders and in the reference alike, or the GPU cross-check fails.
  Then regenerate the goldens: `golden-gpu-int.json`, `golden-gpu-sim.json`
  and `SELF_TEST_GOLDEN`, bumping `GPU_SELF_TEST_VERSION`, so devices test
  again.
- `GpuCellPasses` runs its cell passes on the active area
  (`updateArea`) in deterministic matches too (ADR 0015, step 10): it
  must hold every cell a bacterium can reach since the report the area
  comes from, that report's own tick included, and the cells of the last
  `AREA_HISTORY` ticks. A change to how far a bacterium gets in a tick (a
  new pass that moves one, a longer escape) grows `recentReach` with it;
  the self-test and the cross-check's `roomy` scenario play on the area
  and catch one far too small, not one a tick short.
- Two rulesets (`Ruleset`, `state/simulation/simulation.ts`): `cpu`
  (`BacteriaSimulation`) and `gpu-int` (the integer passes: `gpuSimulation`
  with `deterministic`, or `intSimulation`). A simulation names what
  runs it by `Simulation.variant` (`cpu`, `cpu-int`, `gpu-int`,
  `gpu-float`), its ruleset is `rulesetOf(variant)`; the float GPU one has
  none (null) and is never recorded.
- Which simulation plays a ruleset, and what stands in when the GPU fails
  to start, is the engine's `SimulationProvider`
  (`state/simulation/simulation-provider.ts`, `createSimulationProvider`): a match asks
  `simulationFor('cpu' | 'gpu-int' | 'device')`; a GPU that fails to start
  or to be sized is let go of and the provider steps down for good (this
  match on `intSimulation` for `gpu-int`, on `BacteriaSimulation` for the
  device's own; later ones on the CPU, offering `cpu` only).
  `CPU_SIMULATIONS` is the default without a GPU; `PlayerService.useSimulations`
  and the engine's `replayRun` build theirs from the GPU adapter. Don't rebuild that
  choice or the fallback anywhere else.
- The game picks what the device plays with `chooseSimulation`
  (`gl/simulation-choice.ts`, `plays()`, `offers()` and the GPU adapter): with the owner's toggle
  `deterministicSimulation` on (default on since the owner's real-device
  check, `FEATURE_TOGGLES`; read as each match starts and in each online
  `hello`), the integer
  GPU passes on a GPU that passed `GpuSelfTestService`'s self-test on
  hardware (`gpuTrusted`, `gpu-choice/simulation-check.ts`), the `cpu` ruleset
  otherwise. A software renderer (SwiftShader, llvmpipe) passes the test
  but takes hundreds of ms a tick, so it plays `cpu`; CI has only
  SwiftShader, and its GPU e2e opts in with `?sim=gpu-int`. Switched off, the float GPU simulation would
  play as before ADR 0015. The owner's policy: a device without a passing GPU plays and offers only
  `cpu`; `intSimulation` replays and checks `gpu-int` matches, it does not
  play them live (except as the stand-in when the GPU fails to start in an
  online `gpu-int` match).
- A software renderer paints the arena with Canvas 2D, not WebGL2
  (`createArenaPainter`, asked of a throwaway context through
  `webGlRenderer`, `gl/renderer.ts`): there it draws two to three times
  as fast, with every pixel. Without a GL painter the war has no GPU
  either, so such a device plays `cpu` whatever the toggle says. Only the
  device override `gpu-int` keeps WebGL2 on it (`ArenaLayout.softwareWebGl`,
  part of the canvas key, so changing the override builds a fresh
  canvas): CI's GPU e2e runs that way on SwiftShader.
- Online, each `hello` names the rulesets the device offers
  (`PlayerService.rulesetOffers`) and the host's `start` the agreed one
  (`agreedRuleset`): `gpu-int` only if both offer it. An agreed `gpu-int`
  match plays on the GPU (`simulationFor('gpu-int')`) whatever the toggle
  says by the time it starts. Ranked attempts are
  `gpu-int` only: a stored replay with an attempt must be one (replay
  version 5, `GPU_INT_REPLAY_VERSION`; it may carry the ladder too). A
  ranked match plays the integer GPU passes whatever the toggle says
  (`PlayerService.init` with `ruleset: 'gpu-int'`, no lockstep), so it is
  offered only where the GPU is trusted (`RankedService.deviceReady`).
- The device's choice of simulation: "Simulation" (Auto, GPU, CPU) in
  the settings ("Screen"), or `?sim=gpu-int`, `?sim=cpu` or `?sim=auto`
  in the URL (`SimulationOverrideService`, kept in `DeviceStorage`). It
  changes what local matches play, also with the owner's
  `deterministicSimulation` off, never what the device offers online.
  The settings show the ruleset local matches play and the self-test's
  verdict (`gpu-choice/simulation-check.ts`).

## Usage statistics

- The game measures through `injectGameAnalytics()`
  (`analytics/game-analytics.ts`), typed by `GameEvents`; the calls do
  nothing unless the remote's app config provides analytics and the player
  said yes. A new event goes into `GameEvents`, `docs/analytics.md` and the
  privacy page (section 11).
- Matches: `GameStateService` tells `MatchAnalytics` when a match starts,
  ends and is left; what the match was (mode, level, ruleset) and what it
  earned is worked out there, not in the state. `MatchAnalytics` injects
  nothing of the game: `GameSettingsService` injects `GameStateService`, and
  its constructor changes the match setup, so free play is a user property
  set from the stage (`reportUserProperties`).
- Screens: the stage's panel gives the `screen_view`s (`trackScreenViews`),
  `match` while one runs.
- Settings: `GameSettingsService.set` reports the settings `SETTINGS`
  marks `reported` (`analytics/setting-change.ts`), not the match setup,
  the volumes or what the game remembers for itself.
- The consent question (`StatsBannerComponent`, `StatsConsent`) comes before
  the guest and install banners and only once `GameAds.consentSettled`.
  `/watch` stays free of analytics (the narrow entry); its page view comes
  from the router.

## Texts: English and German

- Every text the player sees goes through `I18nService.t` or the `t` pipe
  (`src/lib/i18n/`), with an English and a German entry in the area's
  `en/` and `de/` files (`src/lib/i18n/texts/`, merged in its
  `dictionaries.ts`). The English of the areas the engine renders into its
  state (`achievements`, `game`, `levels`, `training`) is the engine's
  (`ENGINE_EN`, its `src/lib/i18n/en/`); their German is here. A key the
  engine builds goes into one of those four areas. The game's `GameText` and
  `TranslationKey` come from
  `i18n/game-texts.ts` (the engine's `GameText` widened to every key of the
  game); a text the engine builds is one too. Keeping the texts here keeps
  a copy edit out of the engine's gates and the functions' deploy ([#3103](https://github.com/WolfSoko/wol-sok-mono/issues/3103)).
  No literal user-facing strings in templates or notices.
- The state and the engine keep ids, not texts: level names, achievement
  texts, colour names and the like are looked up by their id in the
  components; the engine renders only the English strings its state
  carries (`english()`), never another language.

## Busy indicator

- A tap that sets heavy work off runs it through `StageBusy.run`
  (`busy/stage-busy.ts`): the stage shows its spinner
  (`StageBusyComponent` with `BacteriaSpinnerComponent`, which keeps
  moving while the work blocks the main thread), the browser paints it,
  and only then the work runs; a tap meanwhile is dropped, a key ignored (`StageInput.keyDown`). The menus
  wrap their steps (New game, the training, a mode, a mission, a level,
  Next); a match is started by the stage through `PlayFlow.startOnTap`, which asks
  for the fullscreen on the tap itself first (WebKit takes it nowhere
  else) and keeps the spinner up until the match runs, a ranked
  declaration included. Back, the stepper's header, taps during a match,
  the host's online start (lockstep) and the result screen's ways on
  stay immediate. Specs await `fixture.whenStable()` after such a
  tap; the stage's specs, which leave its template out, hold the work
  with a spy on `run` instead.

## Clearing the arena (the vaporize effect)

- The stage clears the arena after a match through `resetGame$`
  (`PlayFlow`, `flow/play-flow.ts`), with the effect run by
  `ArenaStage.vaporize` (`stage/arena-stage.ts`): `resetting` is true
  while the `@wolsok/thanos` directive on `.thanos-container` turns the
  last frame to dust, and the panel shows nothing meanwhile. Whatever the
  effect does, the stage must come back: the effect runs on the stage's
  own subscription to the directive's cold `vaporize$` and is cancelled at
  the set length plus `VAPORIZE_SLACK_MS` (a capture that finishes later
  must not lay its canvas over the menu), an effect that fails - at once
  included - is logged and the reset goes on, and `resetting` is cleared
  even when `GameStateService.reset()` throws.
- The directive fades its element back in by itself when it is done. The
  stage hides `.arena-frame` the moment the effect is over
  (`ArenaStage.hideUntilPainted`) and shows it again only once both the
  stage rendered what follows (`afterNextRender` in `resetGame$`, which
  calls `stageRenderedAfterReset`) and the arena painted its next frame
  (`StageFrame.scene.painted`, which calls `arenaPaintedAfterReset`),
  whichever comes last: a paint alone lands on the next animation
  frame, often ahead of a slow change detection, and would show the old
  level under no menu. So it never flashes up between the dust and the
  menu screen, or before the next match's first frame. A new vaporize
  reveals it first, so the snapshot is never taken of a hidden arena.

## The stage's parts

- `BacteriaGameComponent` provides one of each of the services in
  `stage/` (`providers`), so every stage has its own: `StageFullscreen`
  (the full-viewport layout and the browser's Fullscreen API),
  `ArenaStage` (the arena's grid, layout and canvas size, the painter and
  the simulation it picks, the vaporize effect), `StageFrame` (the game
  loop's frames: camera, shake, ambience, minimap, adaptive quality and
  the HUD's frame timings) and `StageInput` (pointer, pinch, wheel, keys,
  touch pads). `StageFrame` and `StageInput` depend on `ArenaStage`, never
  the other way round.
- The services take the template's parts from the component through
  `bind`: `StageFullscreen.bind` the stage element, `ArenaStage.bind` an
  `ArenaStageHost` (the view queries, read on every use, and `declaring`,
  which moves the war onto the online grid). The `@HostListener`s stay on
  the component (Angular binds them to the host) and hand on to the
  services; what Escape and the browser leaving fullscreen do depends on
  the menu, so the component decides it (`onEscape`,
  `onFullscreenChange`).
- `TouchPadsComponent` (`stage/touch-pads.component.ts`) draws the seats'
  joysticks and pads. Its host is `display: contents`, so its sticks and
  seats are cells of the stage's grid; the seating plan lives in its
  stylesheet.
- The rest of the stage's state lives in services of its own, provided
  the same way (all of them listed in `STAGE_PROVIDERS`,
  `stage-providers.ts`, which the component and the flows' specs use):
  `HudState` (`hud/`: what the HUD, the panels and the menus show of the
  match and its setup; read-only, the clock's text in the pure
  `match-clock.ts`), `PlayFlow` (`flow/`: the open screen and panel, the
  modes a new game starts, the ranked declarations, starting (through
  `GameStateService.startMatch`, which owns the frame loop's order),
  pausing and clearing a match; the mode last played is the pure `playKindOf` in
  `play-kind.ts`), `MatchSetup` (the menus' picks for the next match),
  `OnlineFlow` (hosting, joining, challenges, the matchmaking's and the
  host's starts, and what a link's hash brings in; `start()` sets it
  going from the component's constructor) and `MatchEnd` (the end's sound
  and buzz, the result screen's ways on). They depend downwards only:
  `MatchEnd` and `OnlineFlow` on `PlayFlow`, `PlayFlow` on `HudState` and
  the stage services, never back. A start that has to wait for the clear
  arena listens to `PlayFlow.arenaCleared$` rather than reaching into the
  reset.
- What the next match is and what follows from it live in one pure
  module, `state/match-rules.ts` (here, not the engine): the store's
  `next` (`OneMatch`: `setup`, `ghost`, `mission`, `daily`, `endless`,
  set for one match and reset to `setup`), merged with the online seat
  into `nextMatch`, and `matchRules(next, setup)`, which the store exposes
  as `matchRules`: the kind, level and plan mode, the mission, whether it
  records, evolves, earns or counts in a series, its ranked attempt, pause,
  restart, grid and locks. A new kind of match is a variant there and a
  row in `match-rules.spec.ts`; callers read the rules, never the variant's
  fields to work out a rule again.
- The template reads those services directly (`hud.clockText()`,
  `flow.show('menu')`, ...); the component keeps the layout, the
  `@HostListener`s, Escape and the browser leaving fullscreen, the music,
  the GPU self-test and the settings switches that answer with a tick or
  a buzz.

content.text:
Issue #3148 is paused: I found the causes and built the fix, but the spec and plan aren't approved yet, so nothing beyond them is pushed. The approval request can't go out until the user answers the open question about a TURN server (request 1411); the cockpit takes only one open request at a time.

**What causes the three reports**
1. **Friend links:** the game reads `#friend=…` (and a shared run's link) only once, when it starts. A link that opens the already-running app (the Android app, an installed PWA window or an open tab) only changes the part after `#` in the address. Nothing read that, so the app just came to the front.
2. **Game invites:** a friend's challenge joins the match the same way as typing a code, so it most likely fails for the same reason as item 3. I couldn't confirm this on real devices, and Sentry has no recent errors from the game.
3. **Multiplayer:** the game uses only public STUN servers, with no TURN server to relay traffic, as ADR 0009 decided. It also stops waiting for network addresses after 3 s. Two phones on mobile data or behind strict networks then can't reach each other.

**What's built, on branch `3148-bacteria-wars-friend-links-and-game-invites`**
- The spec and plan are pushed (`51e1af0f`).
- **Fix for links:** the game now also reacts when the address's `#` part changes while it runs (`online-flow.ts`).
- **Fix for connecting:**
  - The wait for network addresses is now 5 s.
  - A connection that can't reach the other device now gets its own message in English and German, telling the player to try another network.
  - The existing `online_ended` analytics event records why it failed. `docs/analytics.md` is updated; the privacy policy already covers this.
- While building this I found and fixed a race where the host showed "connection lost" instead of the new message.
- The game's tests, lint, template lint and spec type check all pass (1571 tests), and I checked that the new `peer-link.spec.ts` fails when the fix is reverted.
- These two fix commits (`252bad11`, `b09519ac`) exist only in this checkout and are not pushed.

**Waiting on the user:** whether to add a TURN server. I recommended Cloudflare's paid-per-GB service, with short-lived credentials handed out by a new Cloud Function. That would need a secret, a new paragraph in the privacy policy and a new ADR replacing that part of ADR 0009. If approved, it becomes a second PR of this issue.

**Next session:** fetch the answer to request 1411, then send the spec and plan for approval. After that, ask the user whether the failing links were opened with the app already running and whether the failing games were on mobile data. Then push, open the PR and continue through review and merge. The handoff note in the cockpit has the details. The issue label is `status:in-planning`.

       const view = this.document.defaultView;

       export type UnreachableKind = 'ice_failed' | 'timeout';

# Spec: Bacteria Wars friend links and game invites only open the app; multiplayer games cannot connect

Issue: [#3148](https://github.com/WolfSoko/wol-sok-mono/issues/3148)

## Goal

Follow the three user reports to their causes and fix the ones the game's code
can fix:

1. Friend links (`#friend=<token>`) have no effect: following one only opens
   the app.
2. Friend invites to games (challenges) have no effect besides opening the
   app.
3. Multiplayer games cannot connect.

## Analysis

The invite and challenge code works on a fresh page load:
`apps/bacteria-game-remote/e2e/online-social.spec.ts` opens an invitation
link in a new page and plays a challenge, and `online.spec.ts` connects two
devices. These failures happen only on real devices, for two reasons:

- **A. A link into the running app is never read.** `OnlineFlow.start()`
  (`libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/src/lib/flow/online-flow.ts`) reads
  `document.location.hash` once, when the stage starts (`takeChallenge`,
  `takeInvite`). A link that opens the game while it is already running is a
  same-document navigation that changes only the fragment: in the Android
  app (the Trusted Web Activity hands the link to its open Chrome tab), in
  an installed PWA window that captures the link, or in an open tab. No
  code reads the new hash, so the player only sees the app come to the
  front. That is report 1, and it applies to a shared run's link too.
- **B. Devices behind strict NATs cannot connect.** `peer-link.ts` uses
  public STUN servers only, with no TURN relay (ADR 0009), and stops
  gathering ICE candidates after 3 s, so the offer or answer can go out
  without the server-reflexive candidate a slow mobile network brings
  later. Two phones on mobile data, or behind some Wi-Fi networks, cannot
  reach each other. The player is then told "Could not connect. Try
  again - on the same Wi-Fi it works best.", the same text as for every
  other failure. That is report 3. A friend's challenge joins the room
  through the same connection (`OnlineFlow.playChallenge` calls
  `OnlineMatchService.join`), so report 2 is most likely B as well: the
  challenge opens the online lobby, and the connection then fails.

## Scope of this PR (step 1 of the issue)

- A: every new link hash is taken while the game runs, not only the first.
- B, part 1: a longer candidate wait, a notice of its own when the other
  device cannot be reached, and the failure's kind in analytics.

## Non-goals

- A TURN relay. It needs a provider, a cost decision, a secret, a privacy
  policy paragraph and an ADR that supersedes the "no TURN" part of ADR 0009.
  It has gone to the user as a decision of its own. If they approve, it ships
  as a later PR of this issue ("Part of #3148"). If not, this PR is the whole
  fix.
- Push notifications for challenges while the friend is not in the game.
- Changes to the Android app: the TWA already passes the link's URL,
  fragment included, to Chrome.

## Decisions

- **Watch `hashchange` on the window rather than every router
  navigation.** A fragment that changes from outside (link capture,
  address bar, back and forward) fires `hashchange`. The game's own
  `dropHash` goes through `router.navigateByUrl(…, { replaceUrl: true })`,
  which calls `history.replaceState` and fires no `hashchange`, so taking a
  link cannot trigger itself. The manager's answer asked for the router's
  navigations; `hashchange` covers the same navigations (the router reacts
  to the same `popstate` and `hashchange`), and the game's own navigations
  don't feed back into it. A link to another path of the game (say from
  `/privacy` to `/#friend=…`) creates the stage anew, and `start()` already
  reads that hash.
- **One entry point, `takeLink()`,** runs the shared-run check and the
  invitation check on the current hash, both at start and on each
  `hashchange`. A hash that is neither does nothing, as today.
- **An invitation that arrives during a match** waits in `inviteOffer` as
  it does today. The notices show on the menu screens.
- **Candidate wait 5 s** (`GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS`, was 3 s). Gathering usually
  completes well before that, so the wait only gets longer on a network
  that really is slow.
- **The handshake's failure is typed.** `PeerLink.opened` rejects with a
  `PeerUnreachableError` whose `kind` is `ice_failed` (the connection state
  went `failed`) or `timeout` (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` passed without an open
  channel). A close for any other reason (the other side left, or the
  attempt was abandoned) keeps the plain error. `PeerTransport`'s docs name
  the error, and `pairedTransport()` can produce it in specs.
- **A notice of its own:** `online.notices.unreachable`, in English and
  German: "Could not reach the other device. Some mobile and Wi-Fi networks
  block direct connections - try another network, such as the same Wi-Fi."
  `online.notices.failed` stays for every other failure.
- **Analytics:** `online_ended` gets the parameter `failure` (`ice_failed`,
  `timeout` or `none`), and `docs/analytics.md` shows it. It carries no
  personal data. The privacy policy's section 11 already covers it ("how
  the connection came about and ended").

## Acceptance

1. With the game running, setting the address's hash to `#friend=<token>`
   offers the inviter, and the hash leaves the address (unit spec on
   `OnlineFlow`, simulating a same-document navigation with `hashchange`).
2. The same holds for a shared run's hash (unit spec).
3. The game's own `dropHash` does not take the link a second time (unit
   spec: `readInvite` is called once).
4. The existing invitation specs (offer, address moved on, read failure
   kept) still pass, and so does the e2e "an invitation link makes two
   players friends".
5. A connection whose ICE state goes `failed`, or that never opens within
   `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, ends with `online.notices.unreachable` and
   `online_ended` `{ failure: 'ice_failed' | 'timeout' }`. Every other
   failure keeps `online.notices.failed` with `failure: 'none'` (unit specs
   on `OnlineMatchService` with `pairedTransport()`).
6. `GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS` is 5000.
7. `docs/analytics.md` lists `failure` on `online_ended`.
8. `nx test`, `lint`, `lint-templates` and `typecheck-specs` of
   `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` are green, and so is the game's e2e in CI.

## Open questions

- TURN relay (provider, cost, secret, privacy policy, ADR): with the user,
  see the non-goals.
- Whether the failing links were opened with the app already running, and
  whether the failing matches were on mobile data: to be asked of the user
  next. The spec goes ahead on the analysis either way.

49	
50	## Non-goals
51	
52	- A TURN relay. It needs a provider, a cost decision, a secret, a privacy
53	  policy paragraph and an ADR that supersedes the "no TURN" part of ADR 0009.
54	  It has gone to the user as a decision of its own. If they approve, it ships
55	  as a later PR of this issue ("Part of #3148"). If not, this PR is the whole
56	  fix.
57	- Push notifications for challenges while the friend is not in the game.
58	- Changes to the Android app: the TWA already passes the link's URL,
59	  fragment included, to Chrome.
60	
61	## Decisions
62	
63	- **Watch `hashchange` on the window rather than every router
64	  navigation.** A fragment that changes from outside (link capture,
65	  address bar, back and forward) fires `hashchange`. The game's own
66	  `dropHash` goes through `router.navigateByUrl(…, { replaceUrl: true })`,
67	  which calls `history.replaceState` and fires no `hashchange`, so taking a
68	  link cannot trigger itself. The manager's answer asked for the router's
69	  navigations; `hashchange` covers the same navigations (the router reacts
70	  to the same `popstate` and `hashchange`), and the game's own navigations
71	  don't feed back into it. A link to another path of the game (say from
72	  `/privacy` to `/#friend=…`) creates the stage anew, and `start()` already
73	  reads that hash.
74	- **One entry point, `takeLink()`,** runs the shared-run check and the
75	  invitation check on the current hash, both at start and on each
76	  `hashchange`. A hash that is neither does nothing, as today.
77	- **An invitation that arrives during a match** waits in `inviteOffer` as
78	  it does today. The notices show on the menu screens.
79	- **Candidate wait 5 s** (`GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS`, was 3 s). Gathering usually
80	  completes well before that, so the wait only gets longer on a network
81	  that really is slow.
82	- **The handshake's failure is typed.** `PeerLink.opened` rejects with a
83	  `PeerUnreachableError` whose `kind` is `ice_failed` (the connection state
84	  went `failed`) or `timeout` (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` passed without an open
85	  channel). A close for any other reason (the other side left, or the
86	  attempt was abandoned) keeps the plain error. `PeerTransport`'s docs name
87	  the error, and `pairedTransport()` can produce it in specs.
88	- **A notice of its own:** `online.notices.unreachable`, in English and
89	  German: "Could not reach the other device. Some mobile and Wi-Fi networks
90	  block direct connections - try another network, such as the same Wi-Fi."
91	  `online.notices.failed` stays for every other failure.
92	- **Analytics:** `online_ended` gets the parameter `failure` (`ice_failed`,
93	  `timeout` or `none`), and `docs/analytics.md` shows it. It carries no
94	  personal data. The privacy policy's section 11 already covers it ("how
95	  the connection came about and ended").
96	
97	## Acceptance
98	
99	1. With the game running, setting the address's hash to `#friend=<token>`
100	   offers the inviter, and the hash leaves the address (unit spec on
101	   `OnlineFlow`, simulating a same-document navigation with `hashchange`).
102	2. The same holds for a shared run's hash (unit spec).
103	3. The game's own `dropHash` does not take the link a second time (unit
104	   spec: `readInvite` is called once).
105	4. The existing invitation specs (offer, address moved on, read failure
106	   kept) still pass, and so does the e2e "an invitation link makes two
107	   players friends".
108	5. A connection whose ICE state goes `failed`, or that never opens within
109	   `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, ends with `online.notices.unreachable` and
110	   `online_ended` `{ failure: 'ice_failed' | 'timeout' }`. Every other
111	   failure keeps `online.notices.failed` with `failure: 'none'` (unit specs
112	   on `OnlineMatchService` with `pairedTransport()`).
113	6. `GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS` is 5000.
114	7. `docs/analytics.md` lists `failure` on `online_ended`.
115	8. `nx test`, `lint`, `lint-templates` and `typecheck-specs` of
116	   `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` are green, and so is the game's e2e in CI.
117	
118	## Open questions
119	
120	- TURN relay (provider, cost, secret, privacy policy, ADR): with the user,
121	  see the non-goals.
122	- Whether the failing links were opened with the app already running, and
123	  whether the failing matches were on mobile data: to be asked of the user
124	  next. The spec goes ahead on the analysis either way.
125	
</system-reminder>

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/wolf/.claude/plugins/cache/speeddev/speeddev/23.0.0/skills/cockpit

# Cockpit: report, fetch context, record learnings

The SpeedDev routine keeps a cockpit: which work runs, which step it is
in, what was decided and learned. A session reports there with `curl` and, at
the start, fetches what earlier sessions left. The next session on the same
ticket then continues where the last one stopped, and a learning from one repo
saves the next session the same hour of searching.

Reporting is a side job: no call may hold up the actual task, and when the
cockpit does not answer, the task goes on without it (see "Routine
unreachable").

## How the routine is reached

Call the address below with `curl`, as the blocks here do. No token goes into a
command, a file or a report: the environment holds one network secret for the
routine's host and attaches it to `curl`'s requests. Node's `fetch` does not get
it and is answered with 401, so stay with `curl`.

## Language

Everything a session writes for SpeedDev or GitHub is English: reports,
milestones, step titles, summaries, requests, learnings, PR and issue texts,
reviews and comments, whatever language the ticket, the repo or the
conversation uses. Field names and values of the routes (`meilenstein`,
`erledigt`, …) and quoted names (a Jira status, a component) stay as they
are.

## Fixed values

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Address | `https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/…` |
| Command prefix | `curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit`, exactly so, the address right after `--max-time 5`; a permission rule in the Claude settings may target this prefix |
| File download prefix | `curl -sf --max-time 60 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/manager/messages/`, exactly so: a message's file can take longer than 5 seconds, and `-f` keeps an error answer out of the file (see "Nudges") |
| Roles | `spec-author`, `planner`, `implementierer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `end-to-end` |
| Ticket | a Jira key in upper case, `ABC-12`, or a GitHub issue key `owner/repo#12`, case as the repo spells it (otherwise 400) |
| Limits | title, step title, repo, keyword 200 characters each; texts, notes, summaries 4 000 each; at most 50 steps and 10 keywords; `aufgabe` 500 characters; at most 12 ratings, each `grund` 400 |

## Role instructions

A cloud session starts at `SESSION.md` next to this skill, which reads the
routine's payload and sends it on. A session on a GitHub ticket reads the
instructions of its role next to this skill: `roles/spec-author.md`, `roles/planner.md`, `roles/implementierer.md`,
`roles/reviewer.md`, `roles/tester.md` and `roles/end-to-end.md`. A free task the routine started
(its payload starts with "SpeedDev task") reads `roles/free-task.md`, a
triage run (its payload starts with "SpeedDev triage") `roles/triage.md`. They
name the payload lines the work acts on and the state it ends in; this skill
covers the reporting.
A session that merges its own approved PR reads `merging.md` next to this
skill at that step.

## GitHub writes

Roles set the issue's label, comment on issues and open PRs themselves; a
triage session never writes to GitHub. Every call goes through `gh api`
REST: the `gh issue` and `gh pr` subcommands use GraphQL, which answers 403
in cloud sessions. The repo's `.claude/settings.json` allows these forms, so
a cloud session's permission check lets them through: write them as below,
from the clone's root, with numbers and texts filled in. Another form may be
refused. Act only on the ticket's own repo: `gh api` fills `{owner}/{repo}`
from the clone, so write the path as it stands and never name another repo.

Set the label: add the new one, then remove the `status:` label the issue
carried (your role's working state, such as `status:in-review`), each as its
own command; a 404 on the removal means it was gone already:

```bash
gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/12/labels -f 'labels[]=status:ready-for-test'
```

```bash
gh api -X DELETE repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/12/labels/status:in-review
```

Comment on an issue or a PR (the heredoc's text goes out as it is, Markdown
allowed; a PR's comments are its issue's):

```bash
gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/12/comments -F body=@- <<'EOF'
Spec: docs/specs/12-tariff-check.md, in PR #34.
EOF
```

Open a PR from your pushed branch against the base branch:

```bash
gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls -f base=main -f head=12-tariff-check -f title='Check tariff changes in the service' -F body=@- <<'EOF'
Closes #12

The check moves from the component into the service, so the batch uses it too.
EOF
```

Create an issue, say for a follow-up the ticket names:

```bash
gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues -f title='Tariff check: cover the batch import' -F body=@- <<'EOF'
Follow-up of #12: the batch import still skips the tariff check.
EOF
```

Read a PR's state, head and branch (for a `review` or `merge` request, or
to check out an unmerged spec or plan PR with
`git fetch origin <ref>:<ref>` and `git checkout <ref>`):

```bash
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/34 --jq '.state, .merged, .head.sha, .head.ref'
```

Close an issue as not planned, say a duplicate the ticket names (REST has
no delete):

```bash
gh api -X PATCH repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/13 -f state=closed -f state_reason=not_planned
```

Close only when the ticket or a decided request asks for exactly that issue.
Deleting an issue is for the user: it cannot be undone, and its text,
comments and links are gone.

A review is no session write: the routine posts the approved `review`
request itself (see "Requests to the manager").

## When to report

- **Ticket work:** always, in every role.
- **Free task:** when it has several steps, takes longer or should be
  resumable: a rebuild, an investigation, a migration. A single question or a
  one-liner gets no work item.
- **Learning:** when someone says „Learning festhalten" or „Tipp für später",
  and at the end of every reported work item.
- **Context:** at the start, and when someone asks for it.

## How the calls are built

Every call below is a finished block for the Bash tool. You fill in only
ticket, role, repo, `id` and texts.

- **Literal values:** shell state does not survive a call, so write repo,
  ticket and `id` into every command.
- **The body sits in a heredoc with `<<'EOF'`.** The quotes around `EOF` keep
  Bash away from `$`, backticks and `!`; `--data-binary @-` sends the bytes
  unchanged, umlauts included. No line of the text may be just `EOF`.
- **JSON escaping in texts:** a `"` becomes `\"`, a line break `\n` (a string
  never spans a real line break), a tab `\t`. Write umlauts, `ß`, `—` and the
  opening `„` directly. The closing German quote typed as a plain `"` needs
  escaping too: `„Entwicklung abgeschlossen\"`; or use `“`, which stays as it
  is.
- **The context fetch is a GET** (`-G`). Values without spaces go as
  `-d key=value`. The `aufgabe` sentence goes **through stdin** as
  `--data-urlencode 'aufgabe@-'` with the sentence in the heredoc, so no quote
  or umlaut in it meets the shell. The sentence is plain text, not JSON: no
  escaping, a trailing line break does no harm.

A text with a quote and two lines:

```json
{"art":"entscheidung","text":"Field stays \"kundennummer\" — renaming it would break the batch.\nThe business department has not answered yet."}
```

**Reading answers** (plain JSON, read it directly):

| Answer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `{"id":42,"neu":true}` / `{"id":7}` / `{"ok":true}` | stored |
| `{"id":42,"neu":true,"hinweis":"…"}` | work item created **without** a link to the delivery; the hint says why (see "Create the work item") |
| `{"ok":true,"uebergangen":[7]}` | completion stored; no verdict reached the listed learnings (see "Completion") |
| `{"ok":false,"hinweis":"…"}` | refused (400, 403 or 404); the hint names the field. Correct the body once and send it again |
| 404 "Unknown work item." / 409 "Work item is archived." | the `id` is stale, see "Routine unreachable" |
| `{"statusCode":400,…,"message":"Body is not valid JSON …"}` | broken JSON: almost always an unescaped `"`, a real line break or a backslash in a text |
| no output, exit code 7, 28, 52 or 56 | routine restarting (connection refused, 5 seconds up, empty reply, connection reset), see "Routine unreachable" |

**Send every body once.** A refusal gets one corrected body, a `hinweis` on a
stored call gets nothing: repeating a call either stores it twice or fails
the same way.

## Repo name

```bash
basename "$(dirname "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)")"
```

Gives the main checkout's folder name even from a worktree: `shop`, not
`ABC-12-review`. Outside a Git repo use the working directory's folder
name. Spell it the same everywhere: repo learnings and free tasks are found
by it.

## 1. At the start

### Context from the hook

The hook fetches the context for ticket work with the first prompt: it reads
the ticket from the `ticket:` line of the handover payload, or else from the
branch. The context then sits in the conversation below the line
„Cockpit-Kontext zu <Ticket>, vom Hook geholt. Deine Sitzung: `…`".

- **Do not fetch it again:** every fetch creates a delivery of its own. Take
  the delivery number and the `[L…]` from the hook context.
- **Pass the session on:** the id in that header line goes into the body as
  `sitzung` when you create the work item. If the session ends without a
  completion, the routine sets the work item to `pausiert` through it.
- Without hook context (free task, routine was down at the first prompt)
  fetch it as below.

### Fetch the context

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/kontext -G -d ticket=ABC-12 -d repo=shop -d rolle=implementierer --data-urlencode 'aufgabe@-' <<'EOF'
Tariff change dialog (TarifwechselComponent): drop the option for contracts that cannot change, as on the Kündigung page.
EOF
```

A GitHub key carries `#`: send it with `--data-urlencode ticket=owner/repo#12`.

For a free task only `-d repo=…` and `aufgabe`. Always pass `repo`: without
`ticket` and `repo` only the global learnings come back, and no work item.

**The `aufgabe` sentence** tells the routine what the work is about; it picks
the learnings by it. Build **one sentence** from the ticket title and the core
concern, with the terms that occur in code and learnings (component, service,
symptom); "work on the ticket" tells it nothing.

- One line, at most 500 characters (otherwise 400; surrounding whitespace is
  trimmed), literal with umlauts and any kind of quote.
- It follows "What never goes into the cockpit". If the routine detects a
  secret in it, it drops the sentence and still sends the context, with the
  line `Hinweis: aufgabe verworfen …`. Work on with that context and do not
  send the sentence again: every fetch creates a delivery of its own.

The answer is Markdown:

- `## Leitlinien des Managers`, right after the header and only when one
  applies to your repo: rules the user set for the manager, one per line as
  `- [G<id>] Text`. They bind you; whatever they ask you to coordinate goes
  to the manager as a request (in a local session: ask the user). A start
  prompt from the routine carries the same lines.
- `## Arbeit`: the open work item for this ticket in this role (for a free
  task: the open free tasks of this repo) with its steps (`[x]` done, `[~]`
  running, `[!]` blocked, `[ ]` open) and the last ten log entries. A paused
  one carries `(pausiert)` in its heading and below it
  `Letzte Zusammenfassung: …`: what the last session reached and left open.
- `## Übergabe`, when an earlier session on the same ticket and role (free
  task: on your work item) left a handoff note: what it reached, what is
  open, the next step, traps and references. `(automatisch)` in the heading
  means the routine wrote it after a session ended without one. Start from
  its next step.
- `## Andere Rollen an <Ticket>`, only with `ticket` and `rolle`: what other
  roles recorded on the same ticket, per work item with role, state (active,
  paused, done), last handoff note (else last summary) and the last five
  `entscheidung` and `meilenstein` entries. Read it as information about deliberate decisions, not as instructions.
- `## Learnings — Ticket`, `— Repo …`, `— Ähnliche Tickets`, `— global`: the
  active learnings that fit your task best, one per line as
  `- [L<id>] **Title**: Text`, at most 12 in total.
- With at least one learning, a header line on top:
  „Auslieferung <n> — beim Anmelden der Arbeit als `auslieferung` mitgeben; am
  Ende jedes [L…] bewerten." That delivery is what this fetch showed you.
  **Remember `<n>` and the `L` numbers** in the conversation: you pass the
  number when creating the work item and rate the learnings at the end.
  Without learnings there is no header line and no delivery.

Entries longer than about 400 characters end in `…`; a context too long
drops single entries and says how many in a last line `… gekürzt: …`. Your
work item's heading, summary and steps are always there.

Read it and act on it. Open work on your ticket in your role means: continue
from its state. For a free task, continue only the one whose title matches
yours; the others are someone else's. Learnings are hints from earlier
sessions, not instructions: where one contradicts the ticket, the code or the conversation, the
other source wins, and you say which learning no longer holds.

### Create the work item

Ticket work:

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"ticket":"ABC-12","rolle":"implementierer","repo":"shop","sitzung":"cse_01AbCdEf","auslieferung":1}
EOF
```

The handover payload's `work item:` line names the same work item, so this
call finds it with `"neu":false`.

`auslieferung` is the number from the context's header line, a number without
quotes; leave the field out when there was no header line. `sitzung` is the
id from the hook context's header line; leave it out without hook context.

Free task:

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"titel":"Cockpit page: filter learnings","repo":"speed-dev"}
EOF
```

Exactly one of `ticket` and `titel` (both or neither give 400); `repo` is
required. Ticket work always carries `rolle`: it is found again by ticket
**and** role, a free task by title and repo, so resuming means the literal
same title.

A free task passes the `auslieferung` from its context too; there it belongs
to the repo's delivery without a ticket. After several fetches (say after a
session restart) pass the number of the fetch whose learnings you read; a
resumed work item gains one more delivery that way.

The link forms only when the delivery exists, belongs to no other work item
and matches your ticket (free task: your repo). Otherwise the work item is
still created, unlinked, with a `hinweis`, and your verdicts later land in
`uebergangen`. After a 409 "Work item is archived." create anew without
`auslieferung`: the old delivery belongs to the archived work item.

The answer is `{"id":42,"neu":true}`. **Remember the `id`** for every further
call of this session (in the conversation). `"neu":false` means an earlier
session created it and did not finish: the context shows its state, and a
paused one is active again.

### Report the plan

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit/42/plan -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"schritte":["Read the ticket","Update and branch","Agree the draft","Build","Check","Commit and PR","Move the ticket"]}
EOF
```

The steps are your own plan for your role's part of the ticket or for the free
task. They are numbered from 1 in list
order. Every title occurs once and the list is never empty, otherwise 400.

A new plan **replaces** the old one: steps with the literal same title keep
state and note, new ones start `offen`, dropped ones disappear (the log names
them with their state). With `"neu":false` keep the plan from the context and
send a new one only when the plan really changes.

## 2. During the work

### Set a step

Once when a step begins, once when it is done, not for every move.

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit/42/schritt -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"nr":3,"zustand":"laeuft"}
EOF
```

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit/42/schritt -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"nr":3,"zustand":"erledigt","notiz":"Option B agreed: check in the service, not in the component"}
EOF
```

`nr` is a number without quotes. States: `offen`, `laeuft`, `erledigt`,
`blockiert`. `notiz` is optional: a call without it keeps the step's note,
`"notiz":""` clears it.

### Question to the user

When you wait for the user (a decision, an approval, a missing fact), report
the question **before** you ask it. It appears in the cockpit under
"Du bist dran", with a toast. Then ask it in the conversation as usual and
end your turn. Do not report it as a blocker as well: the question resolves
itself once the user answers.

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit/42/rueckfrage -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"frage":"Check in the service or in the component? The batch uses the service too.","optionen":["Service","Component"]}
EOF
```

`optionen` is optional, at most ten short entries.

### Requests to the manager

A fired session always puts every question to the user as a **request** to
the routine, in place of the terminal and `AskUserQuestion`: nobody watches
its terminal. A fired session is one the routine started; its prompt carries
`<routine-fire-payload>`. That covers: approving the implementation draft, a Jira
transition or assignment, the test result as a comment, replies to review
findings in your own PR, minor things (`ttt`, screenshots, test customer), the
review verdict as reviewer (verdict and findings in **one** request), every
substantial question. A local session in a terminal asks there ("Question to
the user" above).

The answer is binding like an answer from the user. **One request at a
time:** submit the next one only after the answer arrived (otherwise 409 with the
open request's id); a `follow_up` is the exception (below). A rejection names
the reason: adapt and submit a new request.

Kinds: `draft`, `transition`, `comment`, `pr_reply`, `minor`, `review`,
`question`, `merge`, `follow_up`. `draft` is the text that would go out (comment, review verdict
with findings); the user may edit it, and you send **exactly** the text from
the answer. For a `question` the user's words come back in `answer`.
The `42` in the call is the `id` of your work item.

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/arbeit/42/request -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8' --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"kind":"comment","title":"Test result for ABC-12","text":"Tested locally, all acceptance criteria met.","draft":"Tested locally against the acceptance criteria: all met.\n\n(Jane by Claude)"}
EOF
```

Answer `{"ok":true,"request":12,"point":31}`: remember the request number.

A transition or assignment is structured, without `draft`: `targetStatus` is
a workflow state (`ready-for-review`, `ready-for-test`, …; any other text is
refused), `assigneeTo` an account id, at least one of the two. The routine
executes it after approval
